records.title: Data visualisation: charts
records.licence: Summary written for the workshop; the original is under the Open Government Licence v3.0
records.text:
A chart should have one main message, and its title should say what that message is, not only what the data is.

Use a horizontal bar chart when the category names are long, so the labels can be read without turning the head. Sort the bars by size unless the categories have a natural order, such as years. Start the value axis of a bar chart at zero: a bar's length is its value, and a cut axis exaggerates differences.

Label the bars directly with their values instead of relying on gridlines, and avoid legends where a direct label will do. Keep colours few and meaningful: one colour for the bars, a second only to highlight what the text talks about.

Avoid 3D effects, shadows and decoration that do not carry data. Give the source and the date of the data under the chart, and say how the numbers were counted when a reader could count them differently, for example when one record can fall in several categories.

records.title: Contrast and colour (WCAG 2.2, summary)
records.licence: Summary written for the workshop; the original is under the W3C Document License
records.text:
Text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 against its background, and large text at least 3 to 1 (success criterion 1.4.3, level AA). Parts of a chart that a reader needs to understand it, such as bars, lines and the focus outline of a control, need at least 3 to 1 against what is next to them (1.4.11).

Colour must not be the only way information is conveyed (1.4.1). If two series differ only by colour, add labels, patterns or a table, so that readers with colour-blindness, and anyone printing in black and white, can tell them apart.

Every image or chart needs a text alternative that serves the same purpose (1.1.1). For a chart, this is usually a short summary of what it shows plus the numbers in a table. Every form control needs a visible label, and everything must work with the keyboard alone (2.1.1).

records.title: A human rights-based approach to data
records.licence: Summary written for the workshop; the original is © United Nations
records.text:
The guidance note sets out six principles for collecting and using data in a way that respects human rights: participation, data disaggregation, self-identification, transparency, privacy and accountability.

Participation means that the groups described by the data have a say in how it is collected and used. Disaggregation means breaking data down by sex, age, disability, ethnicity and other grounds, so that inequalities become visible. Self-identification means people decide for themselves how they are described.

Transparency asks that the methods, definitions and sources behind the numbers are published, so that others can check them. Privacy asks that data about individuals is protected and that published data cannot be traced back to a person. Accountability means that those who collect and publish data can be held to account for how they do it.
